docs.title: The Vision This Committee Serves
docs.text: A stake where every young single adult is seen, known, loved, and drawn toward Jesus Christ and sacred covenants. This committee unites every married adult serving in the Boise YSA Stake so no one serves alone — anchored to the handbook, the Guide, and the stake's Comprehensive Gathering Plan.

docs.title: Purpose & Charge
docs.text: Established by the Boise YSA Stake Presidency, the committee unites all married adults serving in the stake, including ward leaders, advisors, activities and athletics couples, institute mentors, ministering companions, and stake specialists, into a single counseling body tasked with Training, Sharing, Implementing the Guide and Gathering Plan, Counseling Together, and Reinforcing the Role of YSAs.

docs.title: Membership & Roles
docs.text:
Membership includes every married adult sustained to a stake-serving calling. A Stake Presidency-appointed Committee Coordinator convenes meetings and ensures the annual plan is carried out; three additional roles share specific responsibility:

Role Responsibility Committee Coordinator Sets the agenda, conducts monthly meetings, tracks action items, and reports quarterly to the Stake Presidency. Stake Presidency Liaison Represents Presidency direction, approves the annual meeting plan, and carries counsel back to the Presidency. Committee Members Attend regularly, share honest experience, and apply the Guide and Gathering Plan in their calling.

docs.title: Alignment & Measures of Success
docs.text:
Every training topic is weighed against the Gathering Plan's four priorities: See and Love as God Does, Teach Divine Identity and Potential, Focus on Jesus Christ, and Invite All to Come unto Christ and Make and Keep Sacred Covenants. The committee's monthly training rotates through the Guide in step with this rhythm.

Leading indicators: meeting attendance, best practices shared, adults trained per Guide section, ministering assignments staffed.

Lagging indicators: institute/activity/athletics attendance, temple recommend and temple-night participation, reactivation and new-move-in retention.

docs.title: A Welcome from the Stake Presidency
docs.text:
Dear Brothers and Sisters,

Thank you for accepting this calling. You have been asked to serve among some of the Church's most capable, faithful, and valued disciples, young single adults ages 18 to 35. They are not preparing to become adults. They are adults. They are our brothers and sisters, and the Lord is doing a remarkable work in their lives.

The vision for this stake is simple and sacred: every young single adult is seen, known, loved, and drawn to Jesus Christ and sacred covenants.

Your service will help make that vision a reality. The Lord did not call you by accident. He called you because of your experience, your faith, and your ability to teach and love.

This is a training stake, and it is one of the most joyful assignments in the Church. Many of the young adults here are serving in their first substantial leadership role, and others are serving for the first time in other capacities, such as teaching and music. They are capable and willing. What they often need is a steady role model who will listen, share experience, encourage, and then step back so they can lead.

Please read this guide, study the handbook, and then go be with them. Sit with them. Listen to them. Cheer for them. Love them. Teach them. As you strive to walk beside them, the Lord will magnify every honest effort you make. President Dallin H. Oaks promised those who labor among the rising generation: "As you draw closer to Christ, your students will draw closer to you and to Him. Your capacity to teach the truth they need will increase, and your capacity to love them and discern their needs will be magnified."

We add our witness to his: as you give your heart to this sacred work, you will see the hand of the Lord in their lives and in your own. Great blessings will attend you, your marriage, and your family. Heaven will not leave you to do this alone.

We appreciate the sacred privilege of serving with you.

With gratitude,

The Boise Idaho YSA Stake Presidency

Damon J. Day Chad W. Cleverly Brandon D. Woolf

docs.title: Who We Serve / This Is a Training Stake
docs.text:
Young single adults are unmarried adult members of the Church, ages 18 to 35 (General Handbook: Serving in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, chapter 14, "Single Members," https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/general-handbook/14-single-members). In this stake, they study, work, serve missions, date, wrestle with faith, build careers, seek meaningful connections, and prepare for temple covenants, marriage, and lifelong discipleship. Please speak of them, and to them, as adults.

We say We refrain from saying Young adults, young single adults, brothers and sisters, members of the stake Youth, kids, the kids, my kids, these kids, the youth Leaders, presidencies, activity leads, ministers Helpers, the youth committee, chaperones, supervisors Counsel with, train, support, share experience Run it for them, take over, manage them, keep them in line

This is not a youth calling

Youth programs protect, supervise, and prepare minors. This calling is different. You serve adults. Treat them as peers in the gospel who happen to have less leadership experience than you.

This Is a Training Stake

The Savior increased others' capacity by giving them responsibility and opportunities to grow. He did not do their work for them. He taught, trusted, and then sent them.

The members of this stake are very capable. Most are serving in leadership callings for the first time. Lack of experience is not a weakness to work around. Providing opportunities for growth, experience, and connection is the point of a young single-adult stake.

Our role is to share experience, not to replace theirs. We have seen wards function, councils counsel, activities succeed and fail, and ministering bless people one by one. As a mentor, role model, and teacher, be quick to listen, observe, and quietly offer your experience. Then let them lead.

What training looks like here

We seek to emulate the Savior's example as he taught His disciples. He walked with them, sat with them, and ate with them. He was patient, and he listened.

So, we:

  • Sit beside a presidency, not in front of it.
  • Seek to understand what they are trying to accomplish before we suggest how. First observe, listen, and inquire.
  • Teach from the handbook, not from "the way we did it in our last ward," unless that way is also the Lord's way.
  • After an event or meeting, debrief with kindness: what worked, what we learned, what might be tried next time.
  • Celebrate honest effort. Accept their best work.
  • When something needs to be corrected, do it privately, specifically, and with patience.

docs.title: How We Serve Effectively
docs.text:
Keep these six commitments. They are at the heart of this orientation.

  1. Share your experience. You are here because you have walked farther down the covenant path. First observe, listen, and seek to understand; a young adult is more likely to welcome your counsel once they trust that you have truly heard them. Seek the Spirit before you speak; let Him show you whether this is a moment to offer a story or a moment to simply stay quiet. Offer stories, patterns, and counsel when asked or when the Spirit prompts, and offer them as an invitation to consider, never as a directive to follow. Do not make yourself the expert in the room. Make the handbook and the young adult leaders the experts, and add what you have learned along the way.

  2. Encourage, inspire, and motivate. First-time leaders often underestimate themselves. Listen closely enough to hear what they are actually afraid of, and let that shape how you encourage them. Your confidence in them, offered consistently over time, builds the relationship of trust that lets them take risks. Speak hope. Notice growth. Invite them to stretch, never pressure or shame them into it. Remind them that the Lord qualifies those He calls, and pray for the discernment to see that qualification before they can see it in themselves.

  3. Allow them to lead and fulfill their callings. Delegating is more than giving an assignment. It includes teaching and trusting another person to fulfill it. Build relationships of trust by listening first, understanding how they think and what they need before you hand over a task. If you plan the activity, run the council, or "just handle it," you have taken the calling from them and compelled where you should have invited. Coach. Invite their ideas, invite their questions, invite them to try their own way. Then let them do the work, including the parts that will be imperfect. Seek the Spirit to know when silence is the greater act of trust over intervention.

  4. Correct when needed, with kindness and patience. Doctrine, safety, and handbook principles are not optional. But how you raise a concern still matters as much as that you raise it. Listen first to understand what happened and why before you speak. When something needs to change, speak privately and soon. Be specific. Assume good intent. Invite them to see the change and choose it themselves; do not simply command it. Seek the Spirit, so your words carry correction without wounding. Leave them more confident, not smaller. Never correct a young adult leader in front of those they lead.

  5. Be with them outside of Sunday meetings. Firesides, stake activities, service projects, athletics, and FHE are where names become people and where trust is actually built, not through instruction, but through shared time. Make a genuine effort to attend. Stand among them, not over them. Learn faces. Laugh. Serve. Listen to what they talk about when no one is teaching a lesson. Stay long enough to have a real conversation, and let the Spirit direct you to the conversation that matters most at that time.

  6. Minister one by one. Programs gather people. Ministering turns gathering into belonging. Learn names. Notice who is missing. Listen for what is unsaid as much as what is said. Follow the Spirit to the one. He knows needs you cannot see. Extend an invitation to connect rather than expecting anyone to come to you. Details are in section 6.

docs.title: Begin with the Handbook
docs.text:
The General Handbook is the first and governing resource for your calling. Local plans, including our Boise YSA Stake Comprehensive Gathering Plan, apply the handbook's principles in our stake. They do not replace the handbook. Study these chapters early, then return to them when questions arise.

Handbook Chapter Why it matters in this calling 1–4 Work of salvation and leadership The purpose of every effort here. How the Savior led, taught, delegated, and ministered one by one (General Handbook, chapter 1, "God's Plan and Your Role in the Work of Salvation and Exaltation," https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/general-handbook/1-work-of-salvation-and-exaltation; and chapter 4, "Leadership in the Church of Jesus Christ," https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/general-handbook/4-leadership-in-the-church-of-jesus-christ). 14 Single members Who young single adults are, how they lead, and how wards and stakes support them. Start here. 20 Activities Purpose, planning, safety, and the principle that activities serve people 21 Ministering How assignments work, who owns them, and what it means to watch over and strengthen one another. 25 Temple and family history Covenant progression: the purpose of every gathering we plan. 30 Callings in the Church How callings are extended, how people are trained, and how we help others succeed.

Also, please study Strengthening Young Single Adults, especially the counsel to listen first, understand without judging, and follow the Savior by serving before teaching or inviting ("The Young Single Adult Committee," https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/strengthening-young-single-adults-manual/01-ysa-committee). You can find the handbook at ChurchofJesusChrist.org under General Handbook, or in the Gospel Library app.

A simple rule

When you are unsure, open the handbook with the young adult leader you are supporting. Learning the handbook together is a great opportunity.

docs.title: The Stake Vision and Gathering Plan
docs.text:
The Boise YSA Stake Comprehensive Gathering Plan is the local roadmap for this work. Please review it. You do not need to memorize every calendar item, but you should understand the vision, the four priorities, and the three channels through which we gather.

Vision

A stake where every young single adult is seen, known, loved, and drawn toward Jesus Christ and sacred covenants.

Gathering means reaching young adults and fostering connection and belonging with Jesus Christ and with one another. Reaching includes those who already attend, those who have stepped away, new move-ins, and friends of other faiths. Belonging is connection that precedes conversion. It is created through relationships of trust in which divine identity is affirmed, and covenants are invited.

Guiding principle: every event, league, and class is a covenant-path on-ramp, not an end in itself.

Planning rubric: all activities will be evaluated based on their alignment with one or more of our stake priorities and how it will help a young adult move closer to Christ.

The four priorities

# Priority Application 1 See and Love as God Does Outreach, shepherding, and inclusion. Know them by name. 2 Teach Divine Identity, Purpose, and Potential Education and enrichment. Institute, workshops, mentorship. 3 Focus on Jesus Christ and His Atonement Spiritual depth and healing. Firesides, temple nights, testimony. 4 Invite All to Come unto Christ and Make and Keep Sacred Covenants Conversion and covenant progression. Baptism, temple, calling, marriage.

Three channels of gathering

The plan runs through three coordinated channels. Young adult leaders own the work. All efforts are to be pointed toward Jesus Christ.

Channel Description Stake Activities Monthly stake-wide gatherings plus quarterly signature events: socials, service, adventure, firesides, temple nights, and the annual conference or retreat. Designed so a person arriving alone is seen, welcomed, and connected. Stake Athletics Open-play nights, stake leagues, and inter-stake events. Connection before competition. Every gathering opens with prayer and a brief spiritual thought. A low-pressure on-ramp for newcomers and less-active members. Education and Enrichment Institute as the core engine, monthly enrichment nights, workshops, discussion groups, and mentorship. Threads: Who God says I am. Why I am here. Who I am becoming. How I come unto Him.

Activity Standards

  • It begins with prayer and a brief "why we gather" moment connected to one of the four priorities.
  • A newcomer attending alone can find an instant connection through greeters, hosts, name tags, and mixed-ward teaming.
  • Young adults plan, conduct, and teach. Married couples support and attend.
  • Personal invitations occur before the event. Follow-up occurs within 48 hours after.
  • Someone leaves with a next step: sacrament meeting, institute, temple night, a calling, or a friendship.
  • It is well planned, on time, spiritually grounded, affordable, and newcomer-friendly.

Standards you will hear often

  • Know Them by Name: every young adult on the roster, active and less-active, is personally contacted each month.
  • New move-ins are contacted within 7 days and personally invited to the next ward or stake event within 14 days.
  • Newcomers and absentees are followed up within 48 hours.
  • Elders Quorum presidencies, Relief Society presidencies, and ward mission leaders hold primary responsibility for contacting, welcoming, and ministering. Married couples train, coach, model, support, and befriend. We need to ensure that our efforts do not detract from their opportunity to own and fulfill their stewardship.

docs.title: Be Present, Then Minister
docs.text:
Be with them

Being with our young single adults during Sunday meetings is important, but that is not enough. Being present at events and activities outside Sunday meetings, without an agenda beyond showing up, is one of the best ways to build relationships of trust that enable real ministering. Trust is rarely built through a program; it is built by simply being there, again and again, until they stop wondering why you came.

Make a genuine effort to attend:

  • Firesides and devotionals
  • Stake activities and signature events
  • Service projects
  • Family home evening gatherings
  • Athletics nights and open play, even if you only stay for the opening prayer and a few conversations
  • Institute classes or enrichment nights from time to time

How to be present without taking over

Arrive as a guest and a friend, not as staff. Let young adult leaders greet, conduct, and close; this is itself an invitation to lead, not a hand-off you're merely tolerating. Find the person standing alone. Learn a name. Ask a real question, and then actually listen to the answer rather than moving on to the next greeting. Stay off to the side of the program. If something is going poorly, help the leader succeed rather than stepping up to the microphone; seek the Spirit to discern whether the moment calls for a quiet word to the leader afterward or no intervention at all. The goal is for them to feel stronger because you came, not for the event to run because you did.

Individual ministering

Ministering means serving others as the Savior did. He loved, taught, prayed for, comforted, and blessed those around Him. He listened before He spoke, and He invited people to follow rather than compelling them. In our stake, individual ministering is how Priority 1 becomes personal — and it depends entirely on relationships of trust built one person at a time.

Formal ministering assignments are made by the elders quorum and Relief Society with the bishop's approval. Every single brother is assigned ministering brothers. Every single sister is assigned ministering sisters and ministering brothers. Assignments are made to individuals, not to apartments or groups. A married couple may be assigned to minister together.

Your calling does not replace formal ministering assignments that young single adults have been given. Your efforts are intended to supplement and magnify them. You minister in three ways:

Role Description As a disciple Watch over specific brothers and sisters the Spirit places on your heart. Learn names. Remember details. Pray for them by name. Reach out when they are missing. Let the Spirit, not a roster, tell you who needs you today. As a mentor Offer adult friendship and life experience — work, education, dating and marriage, temple worship, emotional resilience, and discipleship. Mentorship in our stake is intentional, structured, and centered on identity, purpose, potential, and Christ. A mentor listens long before offering perspective, and offers it as counsel to weigh, never as instruction to obey. As a trainer Help quorum and Relief Society leaders see ministering as the central effort of gathering: monthly contact, the 7-day / 14-day welcome, 48-hour follow-up, and prayerful rescue of those who have stepped away. Train them to build trust, listen, and seek the Spirit themselves, rather than simply handing them a checklist to execute.

What individual ministering looks like

  • Learn the names, stories, hopes, and current next steps of the people in your circle of influence.
  • Listen first. Seek to understand without judging or rushing to offer counsel; trust is built in the listening, long before any advice is given.
  • Seek the Spirit before you reach out, and seek Him again in the middle of the conversation. He often changes the plan.
  • Ask about adult life: work, school, roommates, family far away, temple worship, institute, and what they hope for.
  • Invite, do not manage. "Would you come with us to temple night?" is ministering. Checking whether they "should be dating more" is not. An invitation leaves them free to say no; a management question does not.
  • Open your home when it feels natural: a Sunday dinner, an FHE group, a holiday, or a quiet conversation. These informal moments are often where trust deepens fastest.
  • Notice the quiet ones. The Savior sought the one.
  • When needs are serious — worthiness, mental health, safety, finances — love them and walk them to the bishopric, elders quorum, or Relief Society. Avoid becoming a private counselor for what priesthood keys should hold.
  • Keep confidences. Report needs through proper channels, not through hallway conversation. Trust, once broken by a breach of confidence, is very difficult to rebuild.

Adult-to-adult boundaries

  • We are friends and mentors, not parents, chaperones, or social directors.
  • A man and a woman should not travel alone together for Church assignments unless they are married to each other, or are both single.
  • Use wisdom in one-on-one settings. When in doubt, meet as a couple or in a visible, appropriate place.
  • Do not hover at dances or activities as if you were supervising youth.
  • Refrain from commenting on bodies, dating choices, or asking questions like "when are you going to get married?"
  • Correct privately. Praise publicly. Even boundary corrections are more effective when offered as an invitation to adjust than as a rebuke; assume good intent, and leave the relationship of trust intact.

docs.title: Your First 30 Days
docs.text:
Here are some ideas of things you can do to get started.

When What to do Days 1–7 Read this orientation. Read General Handbook chapters 1–4 and 14. Read the opening of the Gathering Plan (vision, four priorities, three channels). Fast and pray for the young adults you will serve. Days 8–14 Meet with the leader who called you or the high councilor who supports your assignment. Learn whom you report to, which young adult leaders you support, and what "success" looks like in the first quarter. Read Handbook chapters 20 and 21. Days 15–21 Attend Sunday meetings and at least one weekday gathering — FHE, a fireside, athletics, or a service project. Learn ten new names. Ask two young adult leaders, "What would help you most right now?" Then listen. Days 22–30 Sit in on a council or planning meeting as a guest. Offer one piece of experience if invited. Identify one brother or sister the Spirit has placed on your heart and make a personal ministering contact. Confirm the next month of gatherings on your calendar.

Questions worth asking

  • How can I incorporate our stake priorities into my own personal ministry?
  • Which of the four priorities could I focus on first?
  • Who has not been seen, known, or invited this month? Prayerfully seek inspiration to "find the one".
  • Who are the young adult leaders I am here to strengthen?
  • What are some things that I can allow young adult leaders to do for themselves?

docs.title: A Closing Invitation
docs.text:
You have been called to help young adults become the leaders the Lord already knows they can be, and to love them toward Jesus Christ while they learn. We have not been called to make our stake look like a well-run youth program.

Please share what you know, then step back enough to let them receive their own revelation. Encourage more than you instruct. Attend more than you announce. Minister more than you manage. When you must correct, do so as the Savior would: clearly, kindly, and with a hand still extended.

Every gathering is an on-ramp. Every name is a soul. Every first-time leader is in training, and so are we.

We are grateful you are here. We love you. The young adults of this stake will be different because you have chosen to see them, know them, love them, teach them, and then let them lead.

Welcome to the work!

Keep this close

  • They are young adults and brothers and sisters, never "youth" or "kids".
  • This is a training stake. Listen, observe, share experience. Let them lead.
  • Encourage, inspire, motivate. Correct privately, with kindness.
  • Be at firesides, activities, service, athletics, and FHE.
  • Minister one by one. Open the handbook.
  • Point every effort to Jesus Christ.

docs.title: Why This Committee Exists
docs.text:
The Boise Idaho YSA Stake Presidency calls married couples as ward leaders, advisors, activity and athletics couples, institute and enrichment mentors, ministering companions, and stake specialists. Each serves faithfully within a separate calling, but often without a shared table for training, counsel, and encouragement.

The Married Adults Committee brings together all married adults serving in the Boise YSA Stake into a single body. It exists so that no one serves alone, so that what one ward or couple learns benefits the whole stake, and so that our combined effort stays anchored to the handbook, the Guide, and the stake's Comprehensive Gathering Plan.

docs.title: Purpose and Charge
docs.text:
The Married Adults Committee is established by the Boise Idaho YSA Stake Presidency and includes all married adults called to serve in the Boise Idaho YSA Stake. Its charge is to:

  • Train. Provide ongoing, practical training for married adults serving with young single adults.
  • Share. Share ideas, successes, best practices, and challenges across wards, callings, and channels.
  • Implement the Guide. Put into practice the principles outlined in A Guide for Married Adults Serving in the Boise Idaho YSA Stake.
  • Implement the Gathering Plan. Carry out the Boise Idaho YSA Stake Comprehensive Gathering Plan across activities, athletics, and education and enrichment.
  • Counsel together. Counsel together regularly to identify and meet the needs of young single adults.
  • Reinforce the role of YSAs. Reinforce the role of young single adults in the stake and how married adults can best teach, minister, mentor, support, and invite them to come unto Christ, keep covenants, prepare for the temple, and develop practical life skills.

The vision this committee serves

A stake where every young single adult is seen, known, loved, and drawn toward Jesus Christ and sacred covenants. Every training topic, shared idea, and agenda item exists to move that vision forward.

This committee mirrors the pattern generally described for young single adult committees: married and single adults counseling together, under priesthood direction, to help YSAs come unto Christ (Strengthening Young Single Adults, "The Young Single Adult Committee," https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/strengthening-young-single-adults-manual/01-ysa-committee).

docs.title: Committee Membership
docs.text:
Membership includes every married adult sustained to a calling that serves the Boise Idaho YSA Stake and is a member of this committee for as long as that calling is held.

Represented Group Typical Callings Included Stake Presidency Liaison High councilor(s) assigned to oversee married-adult service and this committee Ward Priesthood & Relief Society Advisors Married advisor couples to elders quorum and Relief Society presidencies Activities Committee Advisors Married couples supporting stake and ward activity committees Athletics Committee Advisors Married couples supporting stake athletics and leagues Education & Enrichment Committee Advisors Married couples supporting institute partnership, enrichment nights, and mentorship Ministering Couples Married couples with individual ministering assignments among YSAs Stake Gathering Specialists Married specialists focused on outreach, shepherding, and reactivation

docs.title: Committee Coordinator
docs.text:
The Stake Presidency appoints a Committee Coordinator from among the married adults serving in the stake. The Coordinator convenes and conducts committee meetings, coordinates with the Stake Presidency liaison, and ensures the annual meeting plan in Section 7 is carried out.

This is a peer counsel, not a program office

The committee does not run activities, athletics, or enrichment for young single adults; young adult leaders own that work. The committee exists so the married adults supporting them can counsel together, train, and grow more capable as mentors.

docs.title: Roles and Responsibilities
docs.text:
Four roles carry specific responsibility for the committee's work. Every member shares responsibility for showing up, contributing, and applying what is learned.

Committee Coordinator

Sets the agenda with the Stake Presidency liaison, conducts monthly meetings, tracks action items, and reports progress on the Gathering Plan and the Guide's six commitments to the Stake Presidency each quarter.

Stake Presidency Liaison

Represents the Stake Presidency's direction and priorities, approves the annual meeting plan, and carries counsel and concerns from the committee back to the Presidency.

Ward Advisor Representatives

Bring ward-level needs, successes, and challenges to the committee; carry training and best practices back to their ward's married adult advisors and priesthood and Relief Society leaders.

Committee Members

Attend regularly, participate in training, share honest experience, and apply the Guide's principles and the Gathering Plan in their own calling between meetings.

docs.title: Operating Principles
docs.text:
The committee counsels in the same way its members are asked to serve, by observing, listening, and sharing experience rather than directing. These principles, drawn from the Guide's six commitments, govern how the committee operates:

We do We avoid Sit as peers and counsel together Speak as if one couple or ward has the only right answer Share experience as an invitation to consider Turn a shared idea into a directive for every ward Let young adult leaders own their work Plan, run, or take over YSA activities, leagues, or classes Bring challenges with specific, kind counsel Air frustration without seeking a solution together Return to the handbook and the Guide when unsure Default to "the way we did it before"

Councils of this kind exist so members can counsel together, seek revelation for the people they serve, and coordinate the Lord's work in their area of responsibility (General Handbook, chapter 4, "Leadership and Councils in the Church of Jesus Christ," https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/general-handbook/4-leadership-in-the-church-of-jesus-christ).

docs.title: Alignment with the Stake Vision and Gathering Plan
docs.text:
Every committee training topic, discussion, and action item is evaluated against the same rubric that governs the Gathering Plan: does this help a young single adult move closer to Jesus Christ, along one or more of the four stake priorities?

# Priority The Committee's Role 1 See and Love as God Does Train married adults to know every YSA by name and to shepherd the less-active and new move-ins 2 Teach Divine Identity, Purpose, and Potential Equip mentors supporting institute, enrichment nights, and workshops 3 Focus on Jesus Christ and His Atonement Help married adults model Christ-centered presence at firesides and temple nights 4 Invite All to Come unto Christ and Keep Sacred Covenants Coach married adults on inviting, not compelling, covenant progression Channel How Married Adults Support It Stake Activities Attend, support inclusion design, and coach young adult planners — without taking over the planning or conducting Stake Athletics Show up consistently, model sportsmanship, and help team captains shepherd absentees Education and Enrichment Serve as institute ride-share and mentorship partners; support enrichment-night small groups as facilitators

docs.title: Meeting Cadence and Structure
docs.text:
Meeting Frequency Attendees Purpose Full Committee Meeting Monthly All married adults serving in the stake Training, shared best practices, and counsel Stake Presidency Check-in Quarterly Coordinator, Presidency liaison Report progress; receive direction and approval Annual Vision and Planning Retreat Yearly, in August All committee members Review the year; approve next year's meeting plan

Standard Monthly Agenda

Rooted in the handbook's pattern for council and presidency meetings: prepare in advance, counsel together, and close with clear action.

  1. Opening prayer and a brief spiritual thought tied to one of the four stake priorities
  2. Review of action items and follow-through from the previous meeting
  3. Successes: what worked this month, and why
  4. Challenges: what is hard right now, and what counsel is needed
  5. Training topic: one section of the Guide or one Gathering Plan channel, rotated monthly (see Section 7)
  6. Gathering Plan alignment check: are our efforts still pointed at Jesus Christ and the four priorities?
  7. Assignments and next steps, with names and dates attached
  8. Closing prayer

The handbook describes presidency and council meetings as occasions to strengthen individuals and families, prepare in advance, and close with clear direction — the pattern this committee follows each month (General Handbook, chapter 29, "Meetings in the Church," https://www.churchofjesuschrist.org/study/manual/general-handbook/29-meetings-in-the-church).

docs.title: Annual Meeting Plan
docs.text:
The committee's monthly training topic rotates through the Guide and follows the rhythm of the stake's Comprehensive Gathering Plan, so married adults are prepared for what young single adults are experiencing that same month.

docs.title: Stake Gathering Specialist
docs.text:
Combined role — Ward Shepherding & Geographic Stake Liaison

  • Reports To: Stake Presidency (stake calling); works paired with Ward Priesthood and Relief Society leadership, attends ward council, and typically coordinates with the YSA Stake Clerk (records/referral tracking). Ward shepherding is coordinated with the Stake YSA Council's Outreach & Shepherding Co-Leads — the sister specialist with the Sister Co-Lead and the brother specialist with the Priesthood Co-Lead. Geographic Stake Liaison efforts are coordinated through the counselor and high councilor assigned to oversee young single adults.
  • Positions Needed: One married adult couple per ward

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: The Boise YSA Stake Gathering Specialist is the execution layer for shepherding, invitations, and referral coordination for young single adults (ages 18–35). On the ward side, this calling drives the "Know Them by Name" initiative, less-active rescue, and new move-in welcome efforts. On the stake side, it bridges the gap between the YSA Stake and the surrounding geographic ("home") stakes that feed young single adults into the YSA Stake, ensuring referrals don't get lost and new YSAs feel welcomed quickly. Together, these efforts keep communication and personal outreach flowing consistently in every direction — within the ward and across stake boundaries.

docs.title: Category 1: Ward Shepherding
docs.text:
Key Responsibilities

  • Assist with ("Know Them by Name") initiative — every YSA on the ward roster, active and less-active, is contacted monthly.
  • Partner with Ward Priesthood and Relief Society leadership to prayerfully identify specific less-active individuals to reach.
  • Contact new move-ins within 7 days and personally invite them to the next ward or stake event within 14 days.
  • Maintain and reconcile the ward roster against actual attendance.
  • Coordinate with the Ward Representatives (Rep A and Rep B) on follow-up for absentees.
  • Meet monthly with your Outreach & Shepherding Co-Lead — the sister specialist with the Sister Co-Lead, the brother specialist with the Priesthood Co-Lead — to reconcile the ward's portion of the master roster and agree on who needs a personal contact.
  • Report outreach contacts made each month to the Outreach & Shepherding Co-Leads for the Council's combined outreach report, and to the Stake Presidency and High Council for the monthly stewardship review.
  • Regularly meet with other Stake Gathering Specialists to coordinate efforts, share challenges, successes, and best practices.
  • Welcome and assimilate new YSAs into the ward — graduating high school seniors, returning missionaries, and new move-ins alike — coordinating with Young Men/Young Women, seminary, and ward mission leaders to identify them early and extend a personal invitation to the next YSA activity.
  • Track upcoming transitions within the YSA population — including individuals turning 26 (moving between YSA age groupings) and turning 35 (exiting the YSA program) — so each transition is anticipated well ahead of time rather than discovered after the fact.
  • Shepherd YSAs approaching their 35th birthday out of the program with a warm handoff — introducing them to leadership in their next geographic ("home") ward or singles ward before their transition date so no one simply "ages out" unnoticed.
  • Include upcoming new-YSA arrivals (graduating seniors, returning missionaries, move-ins) and age-based transitions (26th and 35th birthdays) in the monthly stewardship report to the Stake Presidency and High Council.

Implementation Ideas

  • Keep a simple monthly contact tracker for each YSA on the roster.
  • Set a 7-day/14-day timer as soon as a new move-in is identified.
  • Bring specific names, not just statistics, to prayerful ward council discussions.
  • Maintain a "Transitions Calendar" tracking upcoming graduation dates, expected missionary return dates, and 26th/35th birthdays so outreach is proactive instead of reactive.
  • Partner with seminary and Young Men/Young Women leaders each spring to get a list of graduating seniors and personally invite them to a YSA activity before they even turn 18.
  • Create a "Welcome Home" checklist for returning missionaries: personal visit or call within their first week home, an invitation to the next activity, and an introduction to ward YSA leadership.
  • Set a reminder 60–90 days before a YSA's 35th birthday to begin transition conversations, including identifying their next ward and personally introducing them to that ward's leadership.
  • Add a "New/Transitioning YSA" flag to the monthly contact tracker so new move-ins, graduating seniors, returning missionaries, and age-based transitions receive extra follow-up touchpoints during their first 90 days.

docs.title: Category 2: Geographic Stake Liaison
docs.text:
Key Responsibilities

  • Serve as the single point of contact between the Boise YSA Stake presidency and the leadership (stake presidencies, YSA-assigned high councilors, and ward-level YSA representatives) of those assigned geographic stakes (approximately 3) that feed young single adults into the YSA Stake.
  • Maintain an up-to-date contact directory of the YSA-assigned leader (counselor/high councilor) and ward YSA advisor/representative in each assigned geographic stake.
  • Facilitate the referral process — ensure each geographic stake has a simple, known way to notify the YSA Stake when a young single adult turns 18, moves into the area, or becomes eligible to attend YSA units.
  • Track referrals through to contact, confirming that every referred individual is reached out to by a YSA ward leader within about one week, and following up if they are not.
  • Push information out to geographic stake leaders — activity calendars, conference dates, institute schedules, and gathering-place information — so it reaches graduating youth and their families.
  • Schedule and help conduct periodic coordination meetings (recommend quarterly) with geographic stake YSA-assigned leaders and ward advisors, similar to the existing YSA committee cadence.
  • Report status and metrics to the YSA Stake presidency on referral volume, response times, and any stakes that are under-referring or unresponsive.
  • Attend Stake YSA Council and stake council meetings as needed to relay geographic-stake feedback and concerns.

Implementation Ideas

  • Set up a shared referral form (via LCR/Church tools or a simple online form) each geographic stake's YSA representative can submit when a new young single adult is identified.
  • Build a basic tracking sheet (spreadsheet or shared document) logging referral date, source stake, assigned ward contact, and follow-up status — reviewed weekly.
  • Establish a named point person (ward YSA advisor or rep) in every geographic stake so communication doesn't rely on ad-hoc contacts.
  • Send a brief quarterly email/newsletter to all geographic stake leaders summarizing upcoming YSA activities, institute offerings, and any process changes.
  • Hold an annual training/kickoff meeting with geographic stake presidencies or their designated YSA leaders to clarify the referral process and answer questions.

docs.title: Appendix: Activity Planning Checklist
docs.text:
For Activity Leads and Ward Activity Coordinators — complete one per activity.

Use this checklist for every stake or ward YSA activity, from a small social to a signature event. Start at least 6 weeks before the activity date (signature events need more lead time). Based on the planning standards in Part 2 of the Boise YSA Stake Comprehensive Gathering Plan.

docs.title: Activity At-a-Glance
docs.text:

  • Date / time:
  • Category:
  • Hosting ward(s):
  • Activity Lead:
  • Checklist started:

Category options: Social · Service · Adventure/Recreational · Signature Stake-Wide Event · Spiritual/Worship · Athletics · Enrichment

Which of the Four Priorities does this activity primarily serve? (check one or more)

Planning rubric

this activity should not be approved until a leader can state which priority it serves and how it moves a YSA one step closer to Christ.

docs.title: Step 1 — Purpose & Priority
docs.text:
• [ ] Stated in one sentence: which priority does this activity serve, and how does it move a YSA one step toward Christ?
  • [ ] Activity type matches a defined category (see options above).
  • [ ] Confirmed this is not scheduled purely for entertainment without a gospel purpose.

docs.title: Step 2 — Inclusion Plan
docs.text:
• [ ] Imagined a YSA arriving alone, new to the area, less-active, or attending for the first time.
  • [ ] Connection Host(s) called, briefed, and assigned to greet and integrate newcomers.
  • [ ] Name tags ordered or prepared.
  • [ ] Structured mingling or mixer activity planned — never left to chance.
  • [ ] Cross-ward teaming plan set, where applicable, to build friendships beyond ward lines.
  • [ ] Cost-conscious design confirmed; subsidy available so no YSA is excluded for financial reasons.

docs.title: Step 3 — Spiritual Framing
docs.text:
• [ ] Opening prayer assigned.
  • [ ] "Why we gather" moment planned — a leader or YSA connects this activity to the Savior and to belonging.
  • [ ] Spiritual thought rotation assigned to a YSA (rotate who gives it, don't default to the same leader every time).
  • [ ] Closing gratitude moment planned.
  • [ ] Next covenant-step invitation identified (institute, temple night, ministering, calling, sacrament, etc.).
  • [ ] Scheduling respects the Sabbath and the sacred nature of Church buildings.

docs.title: Step 4 — Logistics
docs.text:
• [ ] Facility booked and confirmed.
  • [ ] Budget requested and approved.
  • [ ] Equipment and supplies list finalized.
  • [ ] Transportation / carpool plan in place so no YSA is excluded by lack of a ride.
  • [ ] Safety needs addressed where applicable (first aid, release forms, etc.).
  • [ ] RACI written and shared before the event (see table below).

RACI — Who Plans, Funds, Invites, Hosts, Follows Up

Role Name / Assignment Plans (Activity Lead) Funds (Budget owner) Invites (Ward Activity Coordinator(s)) Greets / Hosts (Connection Host(s)) Follows Up (Ward Activity Coordinator(s))

docs.title: Step 5 — Invitation Plan (Pre-Event Outreach)
docs.text:
• [ ] Personal invitation chain started — Ward Activity Coordinators identify target individuals and invite personally, not just by announcement.
  • [ ] "Bring a friend" encouraged and members equipped to invite someone who wouldn't otherwise attend.
  • [ ] Multi-channel reminders scheduled: announcement → group text → personal text → day-of reminder.
  • [ ] Less-active and new-move-in target list reviewed; each person personally invited.
  • [ ] Non-member friends welcome message included, where appropriate.

docs.title: Step 6 — At-Event Belonging (Day-Of)
docs.text:
• [ ] Connection Hosts briefed and stationed near the entrance.
  • [ ] Name tags available at check-in.
  • [ ] Structured mingling activity ready to run.
  • [ ] Cross-ward teams or small groups set.
  • [ ] Attendance tracked, including newcomers, less-active, and non-member guests.

docs.title: Step 7 — Follow-Up Plan (Within 48 Hours)
docs.text:
• [ ] Newcomer and absentee list compiled the day of the activity.
  • [ ] Personal contact made with every newcomer within 48 hours.
  • [ ] Personal contact made with every absentee within 48 hours.
  • [ ] Next-step invitation extended in every follow-up contact.
  • [ ] Patterns of repeated absence flagged to a Stake Gathering Specialist for shepherding outreach.

docs.title: Step 8 — Evaluation (Within 1 Week)
docs.text:
• [ ] What worked well?
  • [ ] What didn't work?
  • [ ] Who attended — new, less-active, and non-member counts logged.
  • [ ] What follow-up is still needed?
  • [ ] Lessons carried forward to the next activity.

Notes:

docs.title: Quality Bar
docs.text:
An activity meets the Boise Idaho YSA Stake standard when it:

  • [ ] Starts on time.
  • [ ] Is well-organized.
  • [ ] Is spiritually anchored.
  • [ ] Is newcomer-friendly.
  • [ ] Stays within budget.

docs.title: Planning Timeline Reminder
docs.text:
• [ ] 6-week planning lead time minimum for regular stake and ward activities.
  • [ ] Longer lead time required for signature stake-wide events (Fall Kickoff Social, Christmas Devotional, YSA Conference/Retreat, Summer Celebration, Year-End Testimony Night, etc.).
  • [ ] Planning sequence: purpose stated → priority identified → inclusion plan → spiritual framing → logistics → invitation plan → follow-up plan → evaluation.

Adapted from Part 2, Sections 1, 4, 5, and 6 of the Boise YSA Stake Comprehensive Gathering Plan (Rev. 1)

docs.title: Appendix: Our Stake Priorities (Quick-Reference Poster)
docs.text:
Four priorities to guide us this season — all centered on Jesus Christ.

  1. See and Love as God Does — Look at every person the way Heavenly Father does — with genuine love and without judgment.
  2. Teach Divine Identity, Purpose, and Potential — Help each young adult know who they are, why they're here, and what they can become.
  3. Focus on Jesus Christ and the Atonement — Keep the Savior at the center of everything we do.
  4. Invite All to Come unto Christ and Make/Keep Covenants — Extend genuine invitations to draw closer to Christ through covenants.

To help these stick, they're shortened to four words:

See Love Teach Invite See each other as God does Love as He loves Identity, purpose, and potential All to come unto Christ

Everything we do flows from — and points back to — Jesus Christ and His Atonement.
